scenario_stem:
Brackmere Paint & Decor is an independent paint and decorating-supplies shop in Country X, owned by Priya Raman for 6 years. It employs 9 staff and sells paint, tools and wallpaper to trade customers and homeowners, generating $680,000 in annual revenue. Current assets are $92,000, including $38,000 owed by trade debtors, while current liabilities are $74,000, including a $30,000 bank overdraft.

Priya has been offered a $150,000 contract to supply paint for a new office block in 4 months, but the client will pay 90 days after the work is completed. She is considering two options: ask existing debtors to pay 30 days sooner in exchange for a 2% discount, or arrange a bank overdraft of $40,000 to bridge the gap.

questions.question_text: Define 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It measures the cash and other short-term assets available to fund day-to-day trading after short-term debts are accounted for [2].

knowledge_max_2: working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities
it represents funds available for day-to-day operations / paying short-term debts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackmere Paint & Decor needs sufficient working capital.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Sufficient working capital allows a business to pay its short-term debts when they fall due [k], which matters because Brackmere's current liabilities are $74,000, including a $30,000 bank overdraft [app]. Reason 2: Working capital keeps a business trading while it waits for money it is owed to arrive [k], as $38,000 of Brackmere's $92,000 current assets is owed by trade debtors [app].

knowledge_max_2: working capital pays short-term debts / liabilities as they fall due
working capital funds day-to-day trading while awaiting payment from debtors
application_max_2: current liabilities are $74,000 including a $30,000 bank overdraft
$38,000 of current assets is owed by trade debtors

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brackmere of asking existing debtors to pay sooner.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Getting cash in from debtors sooner brings money into the business faster [k], helping Priya fund the $150,000 office-block contract before the client pays 90 days after completion [app], which reduces the need to arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft [an]. Benefit 2: Converting $38,000 owed by trade debtors into cash more quickly would strengthen Brackmere's position [k], where current liabilities of $74,000 already exceed the cash balance and current assets of $92,000 leave only $18,000 of working capital [app], easing pressure on day-to-day payments such as wages and suppliers [an].

knowledge_max_2: receiving debtor payments sooner speeds up cash inflows
faster collection improves the firm's cash / working capital position

analysis_max_2: earlier collection reduces reliance on the $40,000 bank overdraft

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should ask existing debtors to pay sooner or arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Asking debtors to pay sooner would inject cash without further borrowing [k], and it directly tackles the $38,000 owed by trade debtors that is straining Brackmere's cash while current liabilities stand at $74,000 [app]. This would help fund the $150,000 contract sooner and reduce dependence on the $40,000 bank overdraft [an]. However, offering a 2% discount would cost money on every early-paying invoice [k], cutting into the $680,000 annual revenue Brackmere currently earns [app], and some debtors may still pay late despite the incentive, so the discount could be paid out without securing faster cash [an]. On balance, for a one-off gap of 4 months on a single contract, the bank overdraft is the more reliable option because it can be drawn down and repaid as soon as the contract client pays [eval]. Brackmere already uses a $30,000 bank overdraft within its current liabilities, so extending this arrangement is a familiar, flexible tool. Overall, Priya should arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft rather than discount debtors, since the 2% discount is a recurring cost while the overdraft is temporary and matches the 90-day payment gap [eval].

scenario_stem:
Darrowmere Marine Engines is a private limited company in Country X, repairing and servicing fishing-boat engines for 8 years. It employs 14 mechanics and turns over $540,000 a year. The workshop serves 30 regular fishing boats each month, with demand peaking before the autumn fishing season. At the end of May, current assets were $61,000 but current liabilities were $78,000, leaving negative working capital of $17,000. The workshop must pay $45,000 for engine parts within 10 days to keep its repair contract with the local fishing fleet.

Managing director Joss Darrow is considering two options: extend the existing $25,000 bank overdraft to $70,000, or take out a $45,000 bank loan at 9% interest per year, repayable over 3 years. Any borrowing would be paid from future repair income.

questions.question_text: Define 'bank overdraft'.
questions.model_answer: A bank overdraft allows a business to withdraw more money than it holds in its current account, up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount actually overdrawn [2].

knowledge_max_2: an overdraft lets the business spend more than its current account balance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Darrowmere Marine Engines needs sufficient working capital.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to meet its short-term debts as they fall due [k], which is critical for Darrowmere as current liabilities of $78,000 exceed current assets of $61,000 [app]. Reason 2: Sufficient working capital keeps a workshop trading without interruption [k], as Darrowmere must pay $45,000 for engine parts within 10 days to keep its fishing-fleet repair contract [app].

knowledge_max_2: working capital pays short-term debts and obligations
working capital funds continuous day-to-day trading
application_max_2: current liabilities of $78,000 exceed current assets of $61,000

questions.question_text: Explain two differences between a bank overdraft and a bank loan as ways to overcome a short-term cash-flow problem.
questions.model_answer: Difference 1: An overdraft is a flexible limit on the current account with interest charged only on the amount used [k], so Darrowmere could extend its $25,000 overdraft to cover the $45,000 parts bill and repay it as repair income arrives [app], which is ideal if the cash gap lasts only a few weeks [an]. Difference 2: A bank loan is a fixed sum borrowed for a set term with interest paid over the whole period [k], so the $45,000 loan at 9% interest repayable over 3 years spreads the cost predictably [app], but Darrowmere would keep paying interest even after the cash crisis has passed [an].

knowledge_max_2: overdraft is flexible, interest only on amount used
loan is a fixed sum repaid over a set term with interest
application_max_2: the $25,000 overdraft could be extended to cover the $45,000 parts bill
the $45,000 loan at 9% interest is repayable over 3 years
analysis_max_2: overdraft suits a gap of only a few weeks as it is repaid quickly

questions.question_text: Do you think Joss should extend the overdraft to $70,000 or take the $45,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Extending the overdraft to $70,000 gives Darrowmere an immediate buffer with interest charged only on what is used [k], matching the $45,000 parts bill due within 10 days and the one-off nature of the gap [app]. If repair income recovers within weeks, total interest would be far below paying 9% on a $45,000 loan for 3 years [an]. However, the bank can demand repayment of an overdraft at short notice [k], which is risky for a firm whose current liabilities of $78,000 already exceed current assets of $61,000, leaving negative working capital of $17,000 [app]. The 3-year loan guarantees the $45,000 and cannot be withdrawn early, though it costs about $4,050 of interest each year plus the fixed repayments [an]. On balance, the bank loan is the safer choice because it cannot be recalled and fixes the repayment schedule while Darrowmere rebuilds its working capital [eval]. The loan also forces disciplined budgeting, whereas an extended overdraft could mask a deeper cash problem. Overall, Joss should take the $45,000 bank loan, since the predictable cost of about $4,050 a year is a fair price for security of funding [eval].

scenario_stem:
Kettleworth Bakery is a family partnership in Country X, operating from a unit on the industrial estate and supplying bread and rolls to 45 cafes and grocery stores for 11 years. It employs 16 bakers and has annual sales of $720,000. The bakery pays flour and packaging suppliers within 30 days and is owed $52,000 by customers on 60-day terms. Current assets are $84,000 and current liabilities are $65,000.

A $120,000 industrial mixer has broken and the bakery urgently needs $30,000 to repair or replace it or lose its wholesale contract. Owner Marta Kettle is considering two options: ask suppliers for an extra 30 days of credit, delaying payment from 30 to 60 days, or arrange a $30,000 bank overdraft at 12% interest a year with the bakery's bank.

questions.model_answer: Creditors are people or businesses to whom money is owed, usually because goods or services have been bought on credit terms and have not yet been paid for [2].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Working capital allows a business to buy the materials it needs for daily trading [k], as Kettleworth must buy flour and packaging and pay its suppliers within 30 days [app]. Reason 2: Working capital allows a business to keep operating while awaiting payment from customers [k], since $52,000 of Kettleworth's money is owed by customers paying on 60-day terms [app].

working capital supports trading while awaiting debtor payments

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Delaying payment breaks the trust that suppliers place in the business [k], so flour and packaging suppliers who currently wait 30 days may refuse the extra 30 days Marta requests, or stop deliveries to the bakery [app], threatening the wholesale contract with 45 cafes and grocery stores that depends on daily supply [an]. Problem 2: Late payment can increase the cost of buying on credit [k], for example through lost cash discounts or tighter terms on the $720,000 of annual sales [app], reducing the bakery's profit on each sale and cutting working capital further [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Marta should ask suppliers for an extra 30 days of credit or arrange the $30,000 bank overdraft? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Asking suppliers for an extra 30 days of credit would preserve Kettleworth's cash without any interest cost [k], which is attractive because current assets of $84,000 and current liabilities of $65,000 leave only $19,000 of working capital [app]. Delaying payment from 30 to 60 days would free up cash to repair the equipment and protect the wholesale contract [an]. However, stretching suppliers risks deliveries being stopped or terms tightened [k], and the bakery depends on daily flour and packaging supplies to serve 45 cafes and grocery stores on $720,000 of annual sales [app]; a single missed delivery could lose customers to rivals [an]. A $30,000 bank overdraft at 12% interest would cost about $3,600 a year in interest , keeping suppliers happy and deliveries reliable, though it adds a permanent finance cost and the overdraft could be called in. On balance, the overdraft is the better choice because supplier goodwill is fragile and the interest of about $3,600 a year is modest compared with losing the wholesale contract [eval]. Overall, Marta should arrange the $30,000 bank overdraft rather than delay supplier payments, since reliable supply matters more than the interest saved [eval].

It employs 26 workers and generates $1,150,000 in annual revenue, supplying offices and clinics across the region. Current assets are $140,000 and current liabilities are $95,000. The company planned to buy an $85,000 computer-controlled sawing machine this year, paying from its own cash reserves set aside for expansion.

Rising timber prices have cut the cash balance to $18,000, and the firm owes $60,000 to suppliers within 3 weeks. Benefit 2: Avoiding the $85,000 bank loan saves $6,800 of interest a year at 8% [k], reducing fixed finance costs that would otherwise eat into profits from the $1,150,000 of annual revenue [app], improving the working capital left after paying current liabilities of $95,000 [an].

Current assets are $118,000, including $64,000 owed by farm customers, while current liabilities are $87,000, leaving working capital of $31,000.

Customer payments have slowed noticeably, and many farms now take 75 days to pay instead of the agreed 45. Owner Ben Fenwhistle must decide soon. He is considering two options: offer a 3% discount to any debtor paying within 20 days, or keep the 75-day terms and borrow $50,000 from the bank to cover operating costs.
